p.src: Meanwhile, when Yan Qing did not return to Li Shishi's house that night, she too began to feel somewhat uneasy. When the chief steward came to inspect the garden, he saw two thick ropes tied beside a willow tree and knew that the pair had escaped; he had no choice but to report the matter to the Grand Marshal. Gao Qiu was startled when he heard the report. His anxiety deepened, and he remained at home, pleading illness and refusing to go out. At the fifth watch the following morning, the Daoist Sovereign Emperor held court and took his seat in the Hall of Literary Virtue. When the civil and military ranks were assembled, the Son of Heaven ordered the screen raised and commanded his close attendants to summon Privy Council Commissioner Tong Guan from the ranks. He asked, “Last year you led an army of one hundred thousand and personally served as pacification commissioner in the campaign against Liangshan Marsh. What was the outcome?” Tong Guan knelt and memorialized, “Last year your servant led the great army forth on campaign and spared no effort. Unfortunately, the weather was hot, the soldiers could not endure the climate and water, and many fell ill; two or three in every ten died. Seeing how badly the troops and horses were suffering, I therefore temporarily withdrew the army and suspended hostilities, sending each unit back to its original camp for training. The Imperial Guard suffered many losses from illness along the road. Afterward an edict was issued, but this band of outlaws refused pacification. Then Gao Qiu campaigned against them with a naval force, but he too fell ill midway and returned.” The Son of Heaven flew into a rage and shouted, “All of you are treacherous ministers who envy the worthy and resent the capable, and you have acted behind my back! Last year, when you led the army against Liangshan Marsh, after only two battles the rebel troops routed your men and horses so utterly that not a scrap of armor or a single rider returned, bringing the imperial army to a disastrous defeat. Afterward, that scoundrel Gao Qiu squandered vast quantities of prefectural funds and provisions, lost countless warships and great numbers of troops and horses, and was himself captured alive and carried up the mountain. Song Jiang and his men spared his life and released him to return. I have heard that Song Jiang's band neither invades prefectures nor plunders innocent people, but seeks only amnesty so that it may serve the state. Yet you incompetent, greedy, sycophantic ministers draw the court's ranks and stipends in vain and have ruined a great affair of state! You are in charge of the Privy Council—are you not ashamed of yourself? By rights you should be arrested and interrogated, but I shall spare you this once. If you offend again, you will not be forgiven!” Tong Guan had not a word to say and silently withdrew to one side. Grand Marshal Su took leave of the Son of Heaven there in the Hall of Literary Virtue. After the court was dismissed, Privy Council Commissioner Tong returned home with shame written all over his face, pleaded illness, and dared not attend court again. Yan Qing then produced the pardon personally written with the imperial brush by the Daoist Sovereign Emperor and showed it to Song Jiang and the others. Wu Yong said, “This time we are certain to receive good news!” Song Jiang burned fine incense, brought out the divination text of the Mysterious Maiden of the Nine Heavens, prayed and made his supplication to the sky, and obtained an omen of supreme good fortune. Song Jiang rejoiced greatly, certain that the matter would succeed. He again troubled Dai Zong and Yan Qing to go and learn the true state of affairs and report back without delay, so that preparations could be made. Dai Zong and Yan Qing returned after several days and reported, “The court has dispatched Grand Marshal Su to bring the vermilion edict in person, together with imperial wine, gold and silver plaques, red and green brocade, and cloth for outer and inner garments, to offer us amnesty. He will arrive very soon!” Song Jiang was overjoyed when he heard this. In the Hall of Loyalty and Righteousness he hurriedly issued orders, assigning men to erect twenty-four ceremonial pavilions all the way from Liangshan Marsh to the borders of Jizhou. Each was decked above with colored silk and hanging flowers, while reed pipes, flutes, drums, and other music were arranged below. Musicians were hired from the nearby prefectures and counties and assigned to the various pavilions to welcome the imperial edict. A junior chief was appointed to oversee each pavilion. Prefect Zhang Shuye came outside the city walls to welcome him, escorted him into the city, and lodged him at the official posthouse. They seek to serve the state in loyalty and righteousness and to leave their names renowned to later generations. Had Your Excellency come in this manner earlier, the state would not have lost soldiers and generals or squandered money and provisions. Once these righteous men submit, they will surely perform distinguished service for the court.” Grand Marshal Su said, “I shall wait here expressly for that purpose. p.src: Song Jiang gave orders for the imperial wine to be put away, then invited the Grand Commandant to take the central seat while all the chieftains bowed and paid their respects. p.src: Several days passed in a flash. When Grand Commandant Su wished to return, Song Jiang and the others pressed him earnestly to stay. Grand Commandant Su said, “You righteous men do not understand the circumstances. Yuanjing came here bearing the Son of Heaven’s decree, and has now remained for several days. p.src: Early the next morning, the carriages and horses were prepared. Song Jiang personally carried a tray of gold and pearls to Grand Commandant Su’s quarters and, bowing twice, presented it to him. Grand Commandant Su would by no means accept it. Only after Song Jiang pressed the gift upon him again and again did he finally accept it. They packed the clothes chests, secured the baggage and saddled horses, and prepared to depart. As for the rest of the entourage, Zhu Wu and Yue He had entertained them throughout the preceding days, providing food and drink according to custom and suited to each man’s capacity for wine. All were also generously presented with gold, silver, valuables, and silk, and everyone was delighted. They likewise presented gold and treasures to Adviser Wen, but he too refused to accept them. Only when Song Jiang insisted on showing him this courtesy did he agree to take them. Song Jiang then asked Adviser Wen to accompany Grand Commandant Su back to the capital. With gongs, drums, and gentle music, all the chieftains of Liangshan Marsh, great and small, escorted the Grand Commandant down the mountain. After crossing Golden Sands Strand, they escorted him more than thirty li farther. Then all dismounted and offered Grand Commandant Su farewell cups. Song Jiang was the first to raise his cup and say, “When our gracious patron returns to behold the imperial countenance, we beg you to speak well of us and support our cause in your memorial.” Grand Commandant Su replied, “Set your minds at ease, righteous men. Since Wang Lun first established this marsh stronghold, then Chao Gai came up the mountain, and now it has passed into Song Jiang’s hands, several years have gone by, and the harm done to nearby inhabitants has been considerable. In my humble judgment, I now wish to exhaust all our wealth in holding a ten-day market to make restitution. Once all is settled, we shall proceed to the capital in our entirety; how would I dare delay? I also beg Your Excellency to convey this humble intention to the imperial hearing and secure us a more generous deadline.” Grand Commandant Su agreed. Taking leave of everyone, he departed for Jizhou with the entire company that had brought and proclaimed the edict.

p.src: A clear breeze swept the jade steps; dew was gathered in the golden basin. In the east the rising sun had just appeared; at the northern palace gate the pearl blinds were half raised. Outside the Nanxun Gate, one hundred and eight gallant men offered their allegiance; before the Xuande Tower, the sovereign of countless years looked upon them anew. Solemn in bearing, they began the rites of court; displaying their mettle, they still maintained the order of an army. Wind, rain, sun, and stars alike beheld the clearing of Heaven’s countenance; thunderbolts and lightning need no longer trouble the might of Heaven’s chastisement. Before the imperial palace every spirit assembled: sages, immortals, Nezha, vajra guardians, Yama kings, judges of the dead, door gods, gods of the year, and even yakshas, ghosts, and demons—all looked up in reverence to the Daoist Emperor. Beneath the phoenix tower all the beasts came to court: tiger cubs, leopards, qilins, suanni lions, prison beasts, golden-winged birds, eagles and rocs, turtles and apes, and even dogs, rats, snakes, and scorpions—all acknowledged Lord Song as their sovereign. Five dragons flanked the sun: Dragon in the Clouds, Dragon Churning the Rivers, Dragon Leaving the Forest, Nine-Dragoned, and One-Horned Dragon; like flood dragons emerging from caves and sea monsters overturning rivers, they followed their companies toward Heaven’s court. A host of tigers left the mountains: Winged Tiger, Ravine-Leaping Tiger, Brocade-Furred Tiger, Flower-Necked Tiger, Blue-Eyed Tiger, Smiling Tiger, Short-Legged Tiger, and Arrow-Struck Tiger; even the Sick Tiger and Tigress followed the ranks and performed their obeisance. Those whose epithets were duke, marquis, earl, or viscount might naturally know the ceremonies of court; but who would have thought that amid the dust raised by the triple acclamation, gardeners, physicians, diviners, artisans, and boatmen too would be admitted? All who bore hair, locks, whiskers, or beard were fit to receive the imperial favor; who could have imagined that scarlet robes and purple seals would alike be bestowed upon a woman, a prodigal, a monk, and a pilgrim? As for empty titles—Commandant, Military Adviser, Prince Consort, Registrar, General, and Vanguard—the offices had long stood in their names; compared with men of old—Hegemon-King, Li Guang, Guan Suo, Marquis Wen, Yuchi Gong, and Xue Rengui—they were those ancient heroes reborn in the present age. There were handsome ones, like the “Fair-Faced Gentleman” adorned with a flower, bearing flute, fan, drum, and banner, ready to sing and dance; and behold the ugly ones, like the “Blue-Faced Beast” wearing a demon’s visage, wielding spear, sword, whip, and bow, skilled in battle and conquest. The tallest rivaled the “Perilous-Road God,” standing a full ten feet; the fiercest resembled General Shi, whose strength could subdue three mountains. Their hair might be red and their eyes blue, yet every one cherished a loyal heart; they might reach the heavens or leap the waves, but never would they tread the paths of wickedness or flattery. Glad now to draw near the sovereign, they were no longer without honor as in former days; through boundless favor they received defensive commissions—truly, on this day, nothing barred their way. Just look: the scholars among this whole band who brandish spears and wield staves far surpass the officials filling the court who deceive the sovereign and harm the people. Today the gallant men rejoiced to meet their sovereign; only now could the imperial house celebrate the winning of worthy men!

p.src: Now the Daoist Emperor and all his officials watched from Xuande Tower as Song Jiang and the men of Liangshan Marsh passed below with their entire retinue. His imperial countenance lit with joy, and he said delightedly to the assembled officials, “These gallant men are heroes indeed!” He could not cease praising and admiring them, and ordered a palace usher to convey his decree that Song Jiang and the others should change into the imperial brocade robes bestowed upon them before coming into his presence. p.src: The ninefold palace gates opened anew, while the phoenix bells rang clear; The heavenly portals swung wide, revealing the majestic dragon robe. The tortoiseshell banquet tables were spread, with vessels of seven treasures inlaid with gold; Qilin-shaped censers stood in rows, burning blended incense tempered with borneol. Crystal cups alternated with amber goblets, and agate beakers stood beside coral chalices. On crimson-jade platters were heaped qilin flesh and phoenix liver; Purple-jade dishes overflowed with swift camel’s hoof and bear’s paw. The peach-blossom broth was pure, filled with shreds of yellow sheep from beyond the northern frontier; The silver-thread sashimi was fresh, sliced from red carp of the southern rivers. Golden goblets brimmed with fragrant wine, while purple-cloud cups shimmered with nectar of jade. Five stands and eight ritual vessels bore delicacies of every flavor. Sweet sugar had been poured into immortal-lion confections, and flour shaped into fragrant, crisp tokens of victory. Five rounds of wine had just been served, and the third presentation of soup was being set forth. The Imperial Academy of Music presented dances worthy of phoenixes, while the Court of Rites arrayed its senior performers. Through the actors’ entrance they came, each part plainly announced. The first, playing the lead, wore a black-lacquered gauze cap glossy as a mirror and an embroidered silk robe that seemed fashioned by nature itself; The second, playing the comic role, wore a belt of rhinoceros horn that had left the water, a silk kerchief patterned with red flowers and green leaves, a long yellow robe over short-shafted boots, and sleeves and lapels densely worked with landscapes; The third, playing the supporting male, wore a netted ball-topped cap and a silk robe patterned with layered victory emblems. He clearly introduced the performance before all others and recited several rare pieces of miscellaneous prose; The fourth, the painted-face role, stirred the crowd with his speech and surpassed all in the extravagance of his makeup; he sang the tunes prescribed by the playbook and followed established forms in jesting and stage business; The fifth, the secondary painted-face clown, played a frantic fool with wild, staring eyes; a bright stripe of makeup crossed his brow, and two colors of white powder were smeared across his face. He wrapped his head in a greasy old kerchief and wore a slovenly motley jacket. Six blows from the clappers caused him no pain, and two strokes of the hempen whip seemed mere sport. These five led sixty-four performers in formation dances and one hundred and twenty musicians in assorted roles, presenting variety plays, impersonating high officials, and acting out lively stage business. Every one wore a blue kerchief and cylindrical cap, and every one a red sash and red robe. They blew dragon flutes and beat alligator drums, their sound shaking the clouds; They plucked brocade zithers and played silver zheng, their melodies startling fish and birds. At the acrobatic spectacles the crowd raised a clamor, and at every jest they cheered in unison. They portrayed all nations coming to court in an age of peace, and the Eight Immortals celebrating a birthday in a reign of harmony; They performed Emperor Xuanzong’s dream journey to the Moon Palace, and Di Qing’s night capture of Kunlun Pass. There were immortal sages and companions of the Way, and there were filial sons and dutiful grandsons. Those who watched could truly fortify their purpose; Those who listened found it sufficient to nurture their nature and feelings. Presently eight principal performers clustered around four beauties, who sang and danced in paired lines while wind and string instruments sounded together. They sang “Audience with the Son of Heaven,” “Congratulations to the Sacred Court,” “Gratitude for Imperial Grace,” and “Joy Before the Palace”—music of an orderly age; They danced “The Drunken Hui,” “The Living Guanyin,” “Lady Liu Qing,” and “Old Bao”—postures of pure decorum. The grand banquet was complete, and every kind of music sounded together. p.src: Meanwhile, officials of the Bureau of Military Affairs submitted a memorial: “Those who have newly surrendered have rendered no service. They must not be granted titles precipitately. Let them first undertake campaigns, establish merit, and then receive offices and rewards in due measure. At present tens of thousands of them are encamped beneath the city walls, which is most improper. Your Majesty may order that, among the troops commanded by Song Jiang and his fellows, those officers originally from the capital who were taken captive be returned to their former posts, while soldiers from the outer provinces return to their places of origin. As for the rest, divide them into five columns and disperse them between Shandong and Hebei. This is the best policy.” The next day the Son of Heaven ordered a commander of the imperial guard to go directly to Song Jiang’s camp and orally deliver the sacred decree commanding Song Jiang and the others to divide their forces and send every contingent back to its place of origin. When the chieftains heard this, they were displeased and replied, “We have submitted to the imperial court, yet have not received so much as an office or title, and already it means to split up and dispatch our brothers in every direction. We chieftains have followed one another through life and death and sworn never to part! If matters must truly be so, we can only return to Liangshan Marsh.” Song Jiang hastily restrained them, then earnestly addressed the envoy with loyal words and begged him to report the matter favorably. When the commander returned to court, he dared conceal nothing and had no choice but to report all the foregoing words to the Son of Heaven. The Son of Heaven was greatly alarmed and immediately summoned the officials of the Bureau of Military Affairs to deliberate. Tong Guan, a commissioner of military affairs, memorialized: “Though these wretches have surrendered, their hearts remain unchanged, and in the end they will bring us grave calamity. In my humble opinion, Your Majesty should issue a decree luring them into the capital, exterminate all one hundred and eight of them, and only then disperse their troops, thereby removing this threat to the realm.” After hearing him, the Son of Heaven pondered in silence, unable to decide. Just then a high minister emerged from behind the imperial screen, clad in a purple robe and holding an ivory tablet. He shouted, “The beacons of war have not yet died down on our four borders, and now the seeds of disaster are sprouting at the center! It is all because of mediocre and benighted ministers like you that the empire of our sacred dynasty is being ruined!” With words alone that could establish a realm and secure a nation, he came to save men who had shaken heaven and earth. But who was the minister who shouted from behind the imperial screen? Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
